verses.context: One sentence sets Jacob against Esau. Esau has just been described settling in Seir with chiefs and kings (36:8, 36:43); Jacob lives in the land of promise, but only as his father did, as a resident without a holding.
verses.grammar: Vayyeshev Yaaqov, ‘and Jacob settled’, uses the same verb as 36:8, vayyeshev Esav, ‘and Esau settled’, so the two brothers' outcomes are placed side by side in matching words. Beerets megure aviv, ‘in the land of his father's sojournings’, uses megurim, from the root of ger, ‘resident alien’, the word God used when he promised this land to Abraham (17:8). Esau's line ends chapter 36 in ‘the land of their possession’; Jacob's begins here in the land of sojourning.

verses.context: The heading ‘the account of Jacob’ opens the last section of Genesis, but the first name after it is Joseph's. He is seventeen, working with the sons of the concubines, and he brings a bad report about them to their father.
verses.grammar: Hayah roeh et echav batson, ‘he was shepherding with his brothers among the flock’, can also be read ‘he was shepherding his brothers’, since et can be either the preposition ‘with’ or the object marker. Many commentators think the ambiguity is deliberate, hinting at the dreams to come. Vehu naar, ‘and he was a lad’, can also mean ‘assistant’ or ‘servant’. Dibbatam raah, ‘their bad report’, uses dibbah, a word that elsewhere describes damaging or slanderous reports (the spies' report of the land in Numbers 13:32). The text does not say whether Joseph's report was true.

verses.context: Israel loves Joseph more than all his sons and marks that love with a robe. The brothers see it, hate him, and cannot speak to him in peace. The family repeats Isaac's favoritism of 25:28, now with twelve sons watching.
verses.grammar: VeYisrael ahav et Yosef mikkol banav, ‘and Israel loved Joseph more than all his sons’, uses the preposition min, ‘from’, in its comparative sense. Ben zequnim, ‘son of old age’, is literally ‘son of old ages’, a plural of state. Ketonet passim, the robe, is discussed in the chapter note. Verse 4 ends with velo yakhelu dabbero leshalom, literally ‘they were not able to speak to him for peace’, that is, they could not give him even the ordinary greeting of shalom. The word returns with bitter irony in verse 14, when Jacob sends Joseph to see the shalom of his brothers.
verses.text: The meaning of passim is uncertain. The Septuagint rendered it with a Greek word for varied or many-colored, which the Latin Vulgate followed and which gave the King James Version its ‘coat of many colours’. Other translations read ‘a long robe with sleeves’ or ‘an ornamented tunic’, following the view that passim refers to the length of the garment, reaching to the palms or soles.

theology.note: The narrator explains Jacob's preference (Joseph was the son of his old age) without excusing it. The verse shows favoritism in the open, and verse 4 shows its first fruit: sons who cannot speak a civil word to their brother.

verses.context: Joseph dreams that his brothers' sheaves bow to his, and he tells them. Their question puts the dream's meaning into words: kingship and rule. Their hatred grows a second time.
verses.grammar: Vayyosifu od sene oto, ‘and they added still more to hate him’, uses yasaf, ‘to add’, the verb behind Joseph's name, which Rachel explained with ‘May the LORD add to me another son’ (30:24). The phrase comes twice (verses 5 and 8), a grim play on the name: the brothers keep ‘adding’ to their hatred of the one whose name means ‘he adds’. In verse 7, three uses of vehinneh, ‘and look’, pull the listener inside the dream. The brothers answer with two infinitive absolutes, hamalokh timlokh and im mashol timshol, ‘will you really reign... will you really rule’, a form that intensifies the verb and here expresses sarcasm and disbelief.
verses.history: Joseph's family are shepherds, yet the first dream is about harvesting grain. The detail fits the story's end: the brothers will bow to Joseph in Egypt when they come to buy grain in a famine (42:6). Dreams were widely regarded in the ancient Near East as messages from the gods, and a dream that set a younger son over his elders would have struck its hearers as a claim to status.

theology.note: Hatred is counted three times in these verses (verses 4, 5, 8), each time increasing. The brothers' sin begins with a feeling they nurse and feed, long before it becomes an act.

verses.context: A second dream widens the first: sun, moon, and eleven stars bow to Joseph. This time he tells his father as well. Jacob rebukes him openly, the brothers are jealous, and Jacob privately keeps the matter in mind.
verses.grammar: Mishtachavim, ‘bowing down’, is a participle, so the heavenly bodies are pictured in the act of bowing. Jacob's question uses another infinitive absolute, havo navo, ‘shall we indeed come’, echoing the brothers' sarcasm. Vayyigar, ‘and he rebuked’, is a strong verb of reproach. Verse 11 contrasts two responses: vayqanneu, ‘and they were jealous’, a Piel of qana, the verb for burning envy or zeal, and veaviv shamar et haddavar, ‘but his father kept the word’, the verb for guarding or watching over. Jacob scolds the dream aloud and ponders it in silence.

theology.note: God is not named, but the paired dreams are the first hint in Joseph's story that God is speaking. Joseph later teaches Pharaoh that a doubled dream means the matter is fixed by God (41:32). Jacob's keeping of the word is the posture Luke describes in Mary, who "treasured up all these things" (Luke 2:19).

verses.context: The brothers are pasturing near Shechem, the city of chapter 34, and Jacob sends Joseph from Hebron to find them. Joseph answers ‘Here I am’, and Jacob sends him to see whether his brothers are well.
verses.grammar: Joseph's reply, hinneni, ‘here I am’, is the answer of readiness Abraham gave God (22:1, 22:11) and Esau gave his father Isaac (27:1). Jacob's command repeats shalom twice: reeh et shelom achekha veet shelom hatson, ‘see the peace of your brothers and the peace of the flock’. The brothers could not speak to Joseph leshalom (verse 4); now he is sent to ask after their shalom. Vayyishlachehu, ‘and he sent him’, is the last time father and son will be together for over twenty years.
verses.text: In verse 12 the Hebrew word et, the object marker before ‘the flocks’, carries scribal dots over its letters, like the word ‘kissed’ in 33:4. Rabbinic interpreters suggested that the dots hint the brothers went to pasture themselves rather than the flock. English translations do not reflect the dots.
verses.history: Hebron to Shechem was a trip of some fifty miles north along the hill-country ridge road. Hebron sits in the hills, so ‘the Valley of Hebron’ has puzzled readers; it may name a valley near the town, below the heights where the family camped.

verses.context: Joseph is found wandering in the field by an unnamed man who happens to know where the brothers went. The small scene keeps the plot moving at the very point it could have stopped: without the stranger, Joseph would have gone home.
verses.grammar: Vehinneh toeh bassadeh, ‘and look, wandering in the field’, uses a participle of taah, ‘to wander, stray’, the verb used of Hagar in the wilderness (21:14). Mah tevaqqesh, ‘what are you seeking?’, and Joseph's reply, et achai anokhi mevaqqesh, ‘my brothers I am seeking’, place ‘my brothers’ first for emphasis. Dotaynah, ‘toward Dothan’, has the directional ending -ah, and the place name also appears as Dothayin.
verses.history: Dothan is identified with Tell Dothan, north of Shechem at the edge of the plain that leads toward the coastal road. Excavations there in the mid-twentieth century uncovered a walled town occupied over long periods. Dothan appears again when the Arameans surround Elisha there (2 Kings 6:13-17). Jewish tradition preserved by Rashi identified the man in the field as an angel, reading providence into a figure the text leaves unnamed.

theology.note: The anonymous man is the kind of detail Genesis uses to show God's hand without naming it. The chance encounter sends Joseph to Dothan, the caravan route, and Egypt.

verses.context: The brothers see Joseph far off and plan his death before he reaches them. Their words mock the dreamer and dare the dreams to come true.
verses.grammar: Vayyitnakkelu oto, ‘they plotted against him’, is a Hithpael of nakhal, a verb for scheming or acting deceitfully, used of Midian's treachery in Numbers 25:18. Baal hachalomot hallazeh, literally ‘this master of dreams’, uses baal (‘lord’ or ‘owner’) in an idiom for someone characterized by something, with a rare, emphatic demonstrative hallazeh, ‘that one there’. Their plan includes the exact words, chayyah raah akhalathu, ‘a vicious animal devoured him’, that Jacob will speak in verse 33. Venireh mah yihyu chalomotav, ‘and we will see what becomes of his dreams’, is the sentence the rest of Genesis answers.

theology.note: The brothers plan murder and the cover story together. The chapter shows sin reaching for concealment from the start, as Cain's did when he asked whether he was his brother's keeper (4:9).

verses.context: Reuben intervenes, proposing the pit instead of killing, and the narrator tells us his real aim: to rescue Joseph and bring him back to their father. It is the firstborn's attempt to act as one.
verses.grammar: Vayyatsilehu miyyadam, ‘and he rescued him from their hand’, is stated as a fact before the plan fails, describing what Reuben set out to do. Lo nakkennu nafesh, ‘let us not strike him in respect of life’, uses nefesh as ‘life’. Al tishpekhu dam, ‘do not shed blood’, recalls the ban on bloodshed in 9:6. The purpose clause lemaan hatsil otam miyyadam lahashivo el aviv, ‘in order to rescue him from their hand to return him to his father’, lets the reader into Reuben's mind while the brothers remain unaware.

verses.context: When Joseph arrives, the brothers strip off the robe first, then throw him into the pit. The narrator describes the robe in full at the moment it is taken, and adds that the pit was dry.
verses.grammar: Vayyafshitu et Yosef et kuttanto, ‘they stripped Joseph of his robe’, uses the Hiphil of pashat with two objects, the person and the garment. The robe is then named again in full, ketonet hapassim asher alav, ‘the robe of many colors that was on him’, slowing the moment down. Verse 24 ends with a circumstantial clause, vehabor req ein bo mayim, ‘and the pit was empty, there was no water in it’. The double statement stresses that there was nothing to drink.

verses.context: The brothers sit down to eat while Joseph is in the pit. Years later they will remember his pleading at this moment (42:21). A caravan appears, carrying Gilead's goods down to Egypt.
verses.grammar: Vayyeshevu leekhol lechem, ‘and they sat down to eat bread’, is told without comment, and the calm of the meal is the comment. Amos later rebukes feasting people who "fail to grieve over the ruin of Joseph" (Amos 6:6), using Joseph's name for the northern tribes, a phrase many readers hear as an echo of this meal. Orchat Yishmeelim, ‘a caravan of Ishmaelites’, is followed by three cargo words: nekhot, probably a gum or resin (traditionally tragacanth), tseri, ‘balm’, and lot, often identified as ladanum or myrrh. The same three goods appear in the gift Jacob sends to Egypt years later (43:11), when the brothers go down again, this time to the brother they sold.
verses.history: Gilead, the highland east of the Jordan, was famous for its balm (Jeremiah 8:22, 46:11), and Egypt imported resins and aromatics for medicine, incense, and embalming. Whether camels were in common use as early as the patriarchs is debated. A study of animal bones from the copper mines of the Arabah dated the arrival of domesticated camels there to around the tenth century BC, and some take the camels here as a detail from a later age; others point to scattered earlier evidence of camel use and argue that a few camels in a trading caravan need not be out of place.

verses.context: Judah proposes selling Joseph instead of killing him, and his argument mixes profit and kinship. The brothers agree. Judah's first act of leadership in Genesis is to turn a murder into a sale.
verses.grammar: Mah betsa, ‘what gain?’, uses betsa, a word that often means profit gained by violence or dishonesty (Proverbs 1:19). Vekhissinu et damo, ‘and we cover his blood’, reflects the belief that spilled blood cries out until it is answered (4:10, Job 16:18). Ki achinu vesarenu hu, ‘for he is our brother, our flesh’, uses basar, ‘flesh’, in the sense of blood relation (as in 29:14). Vayyishmeu echav, ‘and his brothers listened’, is the verb for obeying: Judah's voice now carries the family.

theology.note: Judah's appeal to brotherhood saves Joseph's life but not his freedom. The chapter shows how a lesser evil can be chosen for mixed motives, and Judah's later offer of himself as a slave in Benjamin's place (44:33) will undo what he starts here.

verses.context: Joseph is drawn out of the pit and sold for twenty pieces of silver, and he is taken to Egypt. The chapter note discusses who did the pulling and selling; the brothers' responsibility is not in doubt.
verses.grammar: Vayyaavru anashim midyanim socharim, ‘and Midianite men, traders, passed by’, introduces the traders with a participle, socharim, ‘merchants’. The verbs that follow, vayyimshekhu vayyaalu, ‘and they drew and brought up’, have no named subject, so the reader must decide whether ‘they’ means the brothers or the Midianites. Beesrim kasef, ‘for twenty of silver’, omits the unit, which is understood as shekels, weights of silver rather than coins.
verses.history: Twenty shekels matches the value the law later sets for a male between five and twenty years old (Leviticus 27:5). The Egyptologist Kenneth Kitchen argued that it also fits recorded slave prices of the early second millennium BC, which rose in later centuries (Exodus 21:32 assumes thirty shekels for a slave). Others think the evidence is too sparse to date the story by prices.

verses.context: Reuben returns to the pit, finds it empty, and tears his clothes. His cry to his brothers is about himself as much as Joseph, and the next verse moves straight to the cover-up.
verses.grammar: Vehinneh en Yosef babbor, ‘and look, Joseph was not in the pit’, puts the reader in Reuben's place at the edge of the empty cistern. His words in verse 30 are clipped: hayyeled enennu vaani anah ani va, literally ‘the boy, he is not, and I, where am I going?’, a broken sentence whose final question can mean ‘what am I to do?’ or ‘where can I go?’ He calls Joseph hayyeled, ‘the child’, a tender word that he repeats years later when the brothers are in trouble in Egypt (42:22).

verses.context: The brothers dip Joseph's robe in a goat's blood and send it to their father with a question. The robe that marked his father's love becomes the evidence of his death.
verses.grammar: Seir izzim, ‘a male goat’, repeats the goats of 27:9, where Rebekah prepared goats and Jacob wore goatskins to deceive Isaac. The brothers' words avoid naming Joseph: haker na hakketonet binkha hi im lo, ‘recognize, please: is it your son's robe or not?’ They say ‘your son’, not ‘our brother’. Haker is the Hiphil imperative of nakar, the recognition verb traced in the chapter note, and the question form lets Jacob draw the lie out of his own mouth.

theology.note: Jacob deceived his father with a goat and his brother's clothes (27:9-16), and now his sons deceive him with a goat and his son's clothes. Genesis lets the parallel speak: the sins of one generation are learned by the next, and the deceiver is deceived.

verses.context: Jacob recognizes the robe and reaches the conclusion the brothers planned. He says the very words of their cover story (verse 20); they never have to tell the lie aloud.
verses.grammar: Tarof toraf Yosef, ‘Joseph is surely torn to pieces’, pairs an infinitive absolute with a Pual (passive) perfect of taraf, the verb for a beast tearing prey. The construction intensifies, like ‘torn, torn to pieces’. Jacob repeats the phrase when he refuses to let Benjamin go (44:28), showing that the grief has not left him.
verses.history: Israel's law allowed a herdsman to bring the remains of an animal torn by a wild beast as proof that he was not at fault for its loss (Exodus 22:13). The brothers produce similar evidence for their brother, and their father reads it as a shepherd would.

verses.context: Jacob mourns with every sign of grief and refuses all comfort. The sons who caused the grief join the family in trying to console him.
verses.grammar: Vayyitabbel, ‘and he mourned’, is a Hithpael of aval, ‘to mourn’, describing grief carried out in public rites. Vaymaen lehitnachem, ‘and he refused to be comforted’, uses a reflexive infinitive: he would not let himself be consoled. Jeremiah uses the same pair of verbs of Rachel, "refusing to be comforted" (Jeremiah 31:15), so the father's and the mother's mourning are joined across the Bible. Ered el beni avel sheolah, ‘I will go down to my son mourning to Sheol’, can mean ‘in mourning for my son’ or ‘down to my son’, joining him among the dead.

theology.note: Scripture lets Jacob's grief stand unrelieved for twenty years of the story, based on a lie. God does not hurry the comfort, and the reader, who knows Joseph lives, is left with the tension between what a sufferer knows and what is true.

Sheol, named here for the first time, is where Jacob expects to go in grief. The Old Testament speaks of it without the fuller hope later revealed, and the Joseph story itself will reverse Jacob's despair when he learns that the son he mourned is alive (45:26-28).

verses.context: The chapter ends in Egypt. While Jacob mourns, Joseph is sold again, to a high Egyptian officer. The story has moved from Canaan to Egypt in a single sentence, and chapter 39 will pick it up after the interlude of Judah and Tamar.
verses.grammar: The verse opens vehammedanim makheru, ‘and the Medanites sold’, with the subject placed before a perfect verb, a Hebrew way of marking an action happening at the same time as the previous scene: while Jacob wept, Joseph was sold. Seris, rendered ‘officer’, can mean ‘eunuch’, but in many texts it is simply a title for a royal official. Sar hattabbachim, ‘captain of the guard’, is literally ‘chief of the slaughterers’, a title for the officer over the king's bodyguard, used later of the Babylonian commander Nebuzaradan (2 Kings 25:8).
verses.text: The Hebrew here reads Medanim, not Midyanim as in verse 28. Medan and Midian are both named as sons of Abraham by Keturah (25:2), and the Samaritan Pentateuch and ancient versions read ‘Midianites’ here, which is how most English Bibles translate. The name Potiphar is Egyptian, usually explained as ‘the one whom Ra has given’, and is very close to Potiphera, the name of Joseph's future father-in-law (41:45).

theology.note: The last verse sets Joseph in the house of a powerful Egyptian while his father believes him dead. Joseph later reads this sale as God's sending: "it was to save lives that God sent me before you" (45:5).
